Foundations

1. Thrombus vs. Embolus — Definitions & Types

Thrombus: a mass formed by the coagulation cascade that stays localized to the site where it formed.

Embolus: a substance that enters or forms in the vasculature at one point, then migrates through the blood flow to lodge at another point and produce symptoms. A thrombus that breaks loose and travels — a thromboembolus — is therefore a type of embolus.

Types of emboli (Kemp's working list)

  • Thrombi (e.g., pulmonary thromboembolism) — by far the most common and clinically important type covered in this lecture.
  • Fat / bone marrow emboli
  • Air
  • Amniotic fluid
  • Cholesterol
  • Septic
  • Bullet
  • Mechanical aortic valve fragment
  • Tumor
Why this matters so much
Kemp stresses that pulmonary thromboembolism is extremely common — roughly 1 in 200,000 people in the U.S. die from it each year — and unlike rarer conditions you may never personally encounter (anti-GBM disease, for example), a very good chance exists that you will see patients at risk for PE in practice, across many specialties. He frames this as reason enough to know the topic cold.

Right-to-left shunting: a testable wrinkle

Normally, a venous (right-sided) thromboembolus travels to the pulmonary circulation and causes no systemic harm beyond the lung. But if a patient has a right-to-left shunt — a patent foramen ovale or atrial septal defect — a venous embolus (or air) can cross over into the systemic (left-sided) circulation. This is called a paradoxical embolism.

Air embolism volume threshold
On the right side of the heart, the body can tolerate roughly 100 mL of air without major consequence. On the left side, even one small air bubble can occlude a coronary or cerebral artery branch and cause infarction — a dramatic volume/location asymmetry worth remembering.
Check yourself — 2 questions

A mass of fibrin, platelets, and red blood cells forms within a deep leg vein via the coagulation cascade and remains fixed at that site without breaking loose. What is the most precise term for this structure?

A mass that forms via the coagulation cascade and stays localized to its site of origin is a thrombus. If it breaks loose and travels to lodge elsewhere, it becomes an embolus (specifically a thromboembolus).

A 34-year-old man with a known atrial septal defect develops a deep venous thrombosis of the leg. Several days later he has an acute stroke. Which phenomenon best explains how a venous clot produced a cerebral infarction?

A right-to-left shunt (ASD or PFO) allows a venous embolus to bypass the lungs and cross into the systemic arterial circulation, producing a paradoxical embolism — here causing a stroke.
Vascular Pathology

2. Pulmonary Thromboembolism (PTE)

Description: a thrombus that forms distally — most often in the deep veins of the lower extremities (popliteal, iliofemoral), but occasionally the pelvic veins or, rarely, the upper extremities — then migrates to the heart, enters the pulmonary artery, and impacts within its branches in the lung.

Source

The great majority arise from deep venous thrombi of the lower extremities; occasionally from pelvic veins (e.g., around the prostate or uterus) or, less commonly, the upper extremities.

Risk factors — Virchow's triad

  • Endothelial damage — promotes clot formation. Recent injury (e.g., ankle fracture), post-surgical state, and severe trauma all contribute here; Kemp notes that extensive trauma causes both immobility and direct vascular injury, doubling the risk contribution.
  • Stasis — immobility/reduced mobility (this is part of why patients are mobilized early after surgery), heart failure.
  • Hypercoagulable state — neoplasia (pancreatic cancer is classically associated), obesity, oral contraceptives and pregnancy, and primary hypercoagulable states such as Factor V Leiden (a mutation that eliminates the cleavage site for protein C, so factor V cannot be inactivated).
Kemp's caveat on “deep” veins
Most PTEs arise from deep, not superficial, veins — but he's careful to note this isn't absolute: a small subset of patients with superficial thrombi go on to develop deep venous thrombi too, and occasionally a superficial clot itself can embolize. Real-world pathology, in his words, “is not absolute.”
Check yourself — 3 questions

A 68-year-old woman is immobilized for two weeks after a hip fracture repair. She develops sudden dyspnea. Which combination of pathophysiologic mechanisms most completely explains her elevated risk for pulmonary thromboembolism?

Post-fracture, post-surgical patients have both direct endothelial/vascular injury from trauma and stasis from immobility — two arms of Virchow's triad acting together.

A patient with a known hypercoagulable state develops a lower-extremity deep venous thrombosis that subsequently travels to and lodges within a branch of the pulmonary artery. Which mutation, causing loss of the cleavage site for protein C, is a classic cause of this hypercoagulable state?

Factor V Leiden is a point mutation in factor V that eliminates the cleavage site normally used by activated protein C, so factor V cannot be inactivated, producing a hypercoagulable state.

Which malignancy is classically associated with an increased risk of venous thromboembolism due to a hypercoagulable state?

Pancreatic cancer is well known for its strong association with hypercoagulability and venous thromboembolism (Trousseau syndrome), more so than the other listed tumors.
Vascular Pathology

3. Peripheral vs. Massive PTE — Clinical Presentation

Kemp draws a sharp distinction between two different presentations, which are based on different criteria (location vs. degree/acuity) and are not synonymous.

Peripheral vs. massive/saddle PTE
Peripheral PTEMassive PTE (often saddle)
What it isA small thromboembolus that travels out to the periphery of the lung, sparing the bifurcation/major arteriesA large thromboembolus, classically lodged at the saddle (where the main pulmonary artery bifurcates into left and right), that obstructs roughly ≥60% of the pulmonary vasculature
OnsetSudden shortness of breath from a sudden regional lung abnormalitySudden onset shortness of breath; can progress to sudden death
Chest painPleuritic chest pain (thrombus reaches the pleural surface); possible friction rub if pleuritis developsNot the dominant feature — hemodynamic collapse dominates
PathologyWedge-shaped infarct based at the pleural surface, downstream of the occluded vesselMay not have time to infarct before causing death
LethalityNot very likely to be lethal by itselfOne of the true causes of sudden death
"Saddle" is location, "massive" is size/acuity
Kemp is explicit that these terms are often used together but describe different things: a saddle PTE sits at the bifurcation but doesn't necessarily cross it entirely, while "massive" refers to how much vasculature is obstructed and how acutely the patient presents. A saddle PTE, though, does typically produce a massive presentation because of how much flow it blocks.
The critical clinical point about peripheral PTE
A peripheral PTE itself is not very likely to kill the patient. Its real importance is as a warning sign: diagnosing it is "a chance to diagnose something that could be very important for that patient," because the next PE this patient has could be the massive, lethal one. Missing a peripheral PE clinically (patients may or may not even seek care) forfeits that warning.

Why the classic "red" infarct isn't always red

Pulmonary infarcts are traditionally taught as hemorrhagic ("red") infarcts because the lung has a dual blood supply — the pulmonary artery and the bronchial artery — so the bronchial circulation continues perfusing (and hemorrhaging into) the infarcted zone even after the pulmonary artery branch is occluded.

Real-world variability
Kemp notes that in his own experience, pulmonary infarcts have not always appeared classically red at autopsy — there is real-world variation — but the underlying concept (dual blood supply producing a hemorrhagic pattern) is still the important, testable idea.

Laboratory & imaging workup

  • D-dimer — reflects breakdown of a forming/resolving thrombus. Useful mainly for its negative predictive value: a normal D-dimer makes PE unlikely, but an elevated D-dimer is nonspecific and does not confirm the diagnosis.
  • Helical (spiral) CT and ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan — V/Q mismatch is expected because the embolus blocks perfusion to a ventilated segment of lung.
Check yourself — 3 questions

A patient develops sudden-onset dyspnea and hypotension after a large thromboembolus lodges at the bifurcation of the main pulmonary artery, obstructing an estimated 65% of the pulmonary vascular bed. Which term best describes this presentation?

Obstruction of roughly 60% or more of the pulmonary vasculature, often at the bifurcation (saddle), defines a massive pulmonary thromboembolism, which can cause sudden death.

A patient with sudden pleuritic chest pain and a friction rub is found to have a wedge-shaped, hemorrhagic lung lesion based at the pleural surface, downstream from a small thromboembolus lodged in a distal pulmonary artery branch. Why does this type of pulmonary infarct classically appear hemorrhagic ("red") rather than pale?

The lung's dual blood supply (pulmonary artery and bronchial artery) means the bronchial circulation continues to perfuse and hemorrhage into the infarcted segment even after the pulmonary artery branch is blocked, producing the classic hemorrhagic infarct.

A patient has a small peripheral pulmonary thromboembolus that causes a wedge-shaped infarct but does not require hospitalization. According to the clinical reasoning emphasized in lecture, what is the most important reason to still diagnose this event?

A peripheral PE is not very likely to be lethal on its own, but it identifies a patient at risk for future thromboemboli, one of which could be massive and lethal — making the diagnosis clinically important as a warning sign.
Vascular Pathology

4. Gross & Microscopic Findings, Dating a Thrombus

Gross appearance

A thromboembolus is found wedged within a distended vessel — imagine the clot forced up into the artery and stretching it out. A key gross clue that a clot is an embolus rather than a thrombus that formed in place: the clot's own branching pattern reflects the vessel it originally formed in (e.g., a leg vein), so it will not match the branching pattern of the vessel it is now lodged within.

Thromboemboli can show a variable degree of organization: they may form in the lower extremity and embolize almost immediately, or persist there for some time (undergoing early organization) before finally breaking loose.

Microscopic dating — how old is this clot?

Lines of Zahn — alternating layers of red blood cells and platelet/fibrin/inflammatory-cell-rich layers, produced by the pulsatile pattern of blood flow during clot formation. Kemp notes these are seen more frequently in arterial thrombi than venous thrombi, since the more forceful, pulsatile arterial flow produces a more distinct layering pattern than the comparatively sluggish venous flow.

As a thrombus ages, it undergoes organization/recanalization: granulation tissue (fibrosis plus angiogenesis) grows into the clot from its periphery, forming small new vascular channels through the old thrombus. This is the pathologic substrate for why recurrent, incompletely resolved PTE leads to pulmonary hypertension (below) — the vessel lumen becomes chronically obliterated by this fibrous, partially-recanalized tissue rather than returning to a fully open channel.

Check yourself — 2 questions

A histologic section of an acute pulmonary thromboembolus shows alternating pale bands of platelets/fibrin and darker bands of red blood cells. What are these alternating bands called, and in which vessel type are they classically more prominent?

Lines of Zahn are alternating layers of platelets/fibrin and red blood cells produced by pulsatile blood flow during clot formation; they are classically more prominent in arterial thrombi, where flow is more forceful and pulsatile than in veins.

On autopsy, two thromboemboli of different apparent ages are found in the same pulmonary artery branch. The older one shows fibrosis with small newly formed capillary channels growing into its periphery. What is this histologic finding called, and what basic process does it represent?

Granulation tissue (fibrosis plus angiogenesis) growing into an aging thrombus represents organization and partial recanalization — the substrate for chronic thromboembolic disease progressing to pulmonary hypertension.
Vascular Pathology

5. Complications of Pulmonary Thromboembolism

  • Sudden death — classically from a massive/saddle PTE; Kemp describes this as one of the recognized causes of true, sudden, unexpected death (a person can be walking, the embolus travels to the lung, and they drop immediately).
  • Pulmonary hypertension → cor pulmonale — with recurrent PTE, the thrombus may resolve completely in some instances, but in others it undergoes only partial organization/fibrosis (see above), chronically obstructing blood flow. This forces the right side of the heart to pump against a smaller effective vascular bed (increased afterload/workload), leading to right ventricular hypertrophy and, eventually, right heart failure (cor pulmonale).
The throughline
This complication pathway — incompletely resolved thrombus → fibrotic, partially recanalized vessel → chronically reduced vascular bed → right ventricular strain → pulmonary hypertension/cor pulmonale — reappears as its own named entity ("chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension") in the pulmonary hypertension section below. Recognize it as the same underlying process viewed from two angles.
Check yourself — 1 question

A 40-year-old woman has had three prior episodes of pulmonary thromboembolism, each only partially resolving with residual fibrotic, partially recanalized thrombus in her pulmonary arteries. Which complication is she now at greatest risk of developing as a direct result?

Recurrent, incompletely resolved pulmonary thromboemboli chronically obstruct the pulmonary vascular bed with fibrotic tissue, increasing right ventricular afterload and producing pulmonary hypertension that can progress to cor pulmonale (right heart failure).
Non-Thrombotic Emboli

6. Bone Marrow, Fat, Amniotic Fluid, Septic, Cholesterol & Bullet Emboli

Bone marrow vs. fat emboli

These terms are sometimes used interchangeably, but Kemp draws a distinction: bone marrow embolism is introduction of actual marrow (hematopoietic cells plus adipose tissue) into the blood, whereas a pure fat embolus is fat alone that has undergone some biochemical change and is not quite identical to native marrow fat.

  • Bone marrow emboli — often due to trauma (frequently seen in patients who received CPR, from rib/sternal fractures), or from infarcted bone, such as in sickle cell crisis.
  • Fat embolism syndrome — occurs commonly after long bone fractures, but also after pancreatitis (enzymatic breakdown of fat) and other conditions. Presents with mental status changes (fat reaching the brain), dyspnea (fat in the lungs), and petechiae. Onset can be within hours, though sometimes takes days.
High-yield vignette pattern
A patient with no bony injury who has had CPR, or a patient with a known hemoglobinopathy, found to have marrow emboli at autopsy → think sickle cell crisis with bone infarction as the source, not trauma.

Amniotic fluid embolism

Occurs during pregnancy (classically peripartum). Histology shows anucleate squamous cells (shed fetal skin) and mucin, which is demonstrated with an Alcian blue stain.

Don't mix up your special stains
Kemp is explicit here: Alcian blue stains mucin. This is a different stain from the one used for amyloid (Congo red) — a distinction he specifically flags as one students commonly confuse.

Septic emboli

Classically arise from endocarditis. A large bacterial load is released from a vegetation all at once and deposits at a distant site; because so much bacteria arrives simultaneously, the host inflammatory response has, in Kemp's words, a "late start" relative to the bacterial burden.

Cholesterol emboli

Occur when an atherosclerotic plaque is disrupted, releasing cholesterol crystals that embolize (frequently to the kidney, as shown above). On routine processing, the cholesterol itself dissolves out, leaving characteristic empty, needle-shaped clefts within the vessel.

Bullet embolism

A bullet or pellet can enter the vasculature and embolize to a site outside the expected wound track. Kemp, as a forensic pathologist, notes this is something surgeons and clinicians should keep in mind: if an entrance wound is found but the projectile itself cannot be located along the expected path, and the patient has downstream ischemia, embolization is a real possibility — a single pellet can be lethal if it lodges somewhere critical (he describes a case of a birdshot pellet embolizing to the coronary circulation and causing death after a shotgun injury).

Other listed sources (briefly)

  • Mechanical aortic valve fragments can break loose and embolize.
  • Tumor emboli — certain tumors are notorious for invading blood vessels directly, especially renal cell carcinoma and hepatocellular carcinoma; this is a distinct phenomenon from ordinary metastasis.
  • Infected material can also embolize if a ring abscess around a native or prosthetic valve causes the valve itself to break loose.
Check yourself — 3 questions

A patient who received CPR after cardiac arrest is found at autopsy to have small emboli composed of hematopoietic cells and adipose tissue within pulmonary vessels, with no history of long bone fracture. What is the most likely source of this finding?

Bone marrow emboli are frequently seen in patients who received CPR, due to rib or sternal fractures from chest compressions introducing marrow into the venous circulation, even without a long bone fracture.

Three days after a femur fracture, a patient develops acute confusion, dyspnea, and a petechial rash on the chest and axillae. Which of the following best describes the expected underlying pathologic finding?

The triad of mental status change, dyspnea, and petechiae after a long bone fracture is classic for fat embolism syndrome, with fat globules found in cerebral and pulmonary capillaries.

A histologic section of a peripartum patient's lung shows anucleate squamous cells within a pulmonary vessel. A special stain is performed to confirm the diagnosis. Which special stain, and which substance does it detect, is appropriate here?

Amniotic fluid embolism is confirmed by finding anucleate fetal squamous cells and mucin; Alcian blue is the special stain used to detect mucin, and is distinct from Congo red, which detects amyloid.
Vascular Pathology

7. Pulmonary Hypertension

Forms/etiologies

  • Primary pulmonary arterial hypertension
  • Due to left-sided heart disease
  • Due to lung disease and/or hypoxia
  • Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension
  • Due to unclear mechanisms

Mechanisms behind each category

  • Chronic lung disease (obstructive or interstitial) — loss of pulmonary vasculature from fibrosis/tissue destruction decreases the total cross-sectional vascular bed the right ventricle must pump through, increasing right-sided strain and driving hypertrophy/failure.
  • Heart disease — e.g., mitral stenosis: blood struggles to return to the left side of the heart, backing pressure up into the pulmonary circulation.
  • Recurrent thromboembolic disease — as covered above, chronic partial obstruction from organizing thrombi.
  • Autoimmune disease — e.g., rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus, via pleuritis/pneumonitis/fibrosis of varying degrees.
  • Obstructive sleep apnea — among the mechanisms with a less fully elucidated pathway.

Clinical presentation

Chest pain, fatigue, dyspnea on exertion — a fairly nonspecific picture that requires you to actively think of pulmonary hypertension as a possibility rather than expecting a distinctive presentation.

Gross & microscopic findings

  • Gross: pulmonary artery atherosclerosis; right ventricular hypertrophy.
  • Microscopic: thickening of the vessel wall; the classic (though, per Kemp, less commonly actually encountered) plexiform lesion.
Why does the pulmonary artery get atherosclerosis at all?
The pulmonary circulation is normally a low-pressure system, and atherosclerosis doesn't typically develop there. But once pulmonary hypertension sets in, the pulmonary arteries experience genuinely elevated pressures — and hypertension is one of the four major modifiable risk factors for atherosclerosis anywhere in the body. So pulmonary artery atherosclerosis is essentially a secondary consequence of the elevated pressures, not a primary/independent process.
A candid residency anecdote
Kemp notes that despite plexiform lesions being the classically taught, textbook-favorite microscopic finding of pulmonary hypertension, he "hardly ever" actually saw one in residency — most cases he encountered showed a lower/earlier stage of vessel wall thickening instead. His working interpretation of the plexiform lesion is that it represents the vasculature trying to form alternate flow pathways around a point of obstruction, since blood cannot pass directly through that point.
Check yourself — 3 questions

A patient with severe mitral stenosis develops progressive dyspnea and is found to have elevated pulmonary artery pressures. Through which general mechanism does left-sided heart disease produce pulmonary hypertension?

In mitral stenosis, blood has difficulty returning to and filling the left heart, so pressure backs up into the pulmonary venous and arterial circulation, producing pulmonary hypertension.

A patient with long-standing pulmonary hypertension is found at autopsy to have atherosclerotic plaques within the pulmonary arteries, a vessel bed not normally prone to atherosclerosis. What is the best explanation for this finding?

Hypertension is one of the four major modifiable risk factors for atherosclerosis; sustained pulmonary hypertension raises pressure within the normally low-pressure pulmonary arteries enough to promote atherosclerosis there as a secondary consequence.

A lung biopsy from a patient with severe pulmonary arterial hypertension shows a small glomeruloid tuft of disorganized, proliferating vascular channels adjacent to a small pulmonary artery. What is this classic (though, in practice, not always seen) histologic finding called?

A plexiform lesion is the classic glomeruloid tuft of proliferating vascular channels seen in severe pulmonary arterial hypertension, thought to represent an attempt to form alternate flow pathways around an obstructed vessel.
Vascular Pathology

8. Diffuse Pulmonary Hemorrhage

  • Goodpasture syndrome — anti-glomerular basement membrane (anti-GBM) antibody disease, targeting the α3 chain of type IV collagen, with involvement of both the kidney and the lung. When the antibody-mediated disease affects only the kidney it is simply anti-GBM disease; when it also involves the lung, it is called Goodpasture syndrome.
  • Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) — can also cause diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage.
  • Prematurity — can itself cause diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage in a neonate, through a mechanism separate from either of the above.
A genuinely rare but must-know diagnosis
Kemp recalls that one of his own medical school pathology instructors, well into his 70s and deep into his career, had seen only a single case of Goodpasture syndrome. It is rare. But he's explicit that its rarity doesn't reduce its exam importance — quite the opposite: "it's always going to be a good test question" precisely because it has such a specific, recognizable clinical and immunologic signature (anti-GBM antibody against the α3 chain of type IV collagen, combined lung + kidney involvement).

Grossly, lungs with diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage are completely hemorrhagic; microscopically, blood vessels are congested with extravasated red blood cells filling the alveolar spaces throughout the section.

Check yourself — 2 questions

A 24-year-old man presents with hemoptysis and acute kidney injury. Serum antibodies are found against the α3 chain of type IV collagen, and a lung biopsy shows diffuse alveolar hemorrhage. What is this combined renal and pulmonary syndrome called?

Anti-glomerular basement membrane antibody disease directed against the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen, with combined renal and pulmonary involvement, defines Goodpasture syndrome.

Which of the following is a recognized cause of diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage in a premature neonate, distinct from any autoimmune antibody-mediated mechanism?

Prematurity itself is recognized as a cause of diffuse pulmonary hemorrhage in neonates, independent of the antibody-mediated mechanisms seen in Goodpasture syndrome or GPA.
